hese lessons are the essence of what military  doctrine teaches leaders today in regards to maneuver.   Maneuver is not as simple as following a few basic rules. The commander must  determine where and how he will maneuver his force into a position of advantage over the  enemy. The risk is not to place your own force in a position of disadvantage. CHARLES MORGAN was born 9 January 1793 in North Carolina. This  statement is based on his gravestone inscription and the 1850 census.   He married Mary Ham, born 17 March 1803 in South Carolina, the daughter  of Joshua and Mary Ham*. Charles and Mary were probably married in  Bedford County, Tennessee where her parents lived in 1820 and 1830 but  no marriage records are available for that period.   I believe they lived in Bedford County, Tennessee in the 1830 census -  two dwellings from Joshua and Mary Ham.

they lived in Bedford County, Tennessee in the 1830 census -  two dwellings from Joshua and Mary Ham. I have not found them in 1840.  Sometime between 1840 and 1850 they moved to Pike County, Illinois where  they lived in the 1850 census. They evidently followed her brother,  James Ham, who emigrated there from Tennessee in the 1830' s.   Charles Morgan died 15 December 1851, aged 58 years, 11 months, 6 days.  He is buried in the Ham Cemetery, Pike County, Illinois. This cemetery  is a 1/4 acre plot high on a bluff overlooking the Illinois River. It  is north of Valley City and about two miles south of Chambersburg. There  have been no burials since 1907. The story of the great seamen of  Elizabeth's reign — Drake, Hawkins, and Frobisher —  is almost the history of the England of their day ; the  battles they fought made the settlements in Virginia and  Massachusetts possible.   Of no less influence in the development of the English  colonial settlements were the naval undertakings of Sir  Henry Morgan in the seventeenth, and of Admiral Ver/  non and Admiral Rodney in the eighteenth, century. rge Washington surveyed the land  holdings of Lord Fairfax in the western region of the Virginia Colony to establish boundaries  between Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania. During this expedition, they completed surveys  and maps for nearly 200 parcels of land that now comprise the eastern neck of the state of West  Virginia. Washington and David Morgan then surveyed and mapped land that Washington had  inherited on the Ohio River. After Washington departed to join the Virginia Regiment in the  British colonial Army late in 1752, David mapped the entire course of the Ohio River that now  serves as the western boundary of West Virginia. During their surveying work, Washington met  David’s younger brother Zackquill (Zack) Morgan, and established a long-standing relationship. Gilbert, the senior seaman in the group, led a flotilla of seven ships that set sail in November  1578 from Plymouth to scout for colony sites. Miles Morgan captained his ship, Red Lion of  Newport, with a crew of 48 men and the investor Knollys who traveled with his own entourage  of five militia, in case of “engagement with hostiles upon landfall.” One of the other ships, the  Ann Ager, was captained by Raleigh, and Gilbert captained the flagship Falcon, contributed by  the Queen. Grenville and three of his most experienced captains helmed the other four ships.  Early in the voyage, Miles ran afoul of Knollys who felt that Miles had deceived him

bert hustled over in the Falcon to stop the dispute, promised Knollys a more substantial cut  of any profits, and transferred the irascible investor to the Falcon.    Six weeks out, storms enveloped the fleet, damaging several, and causing all of the ships to  return to Plymouth except the Red Lion. The last flag signal Gilbert received from Miles Morgan  on the Red Lion indicated that they were pressing ahead. The Red Lion was never seen again. WF and Thomas arrived at the Hackleman termination campsite near present-day Portland on  September 23, 1845, about five months after departure. Along the way 11 travellers lost their  lives (11/303; 3.6%), much lower than the average ten percent mortality rate along the Oregon  Trail during the early years of westward emigration. During the first month, while still in the  Kansas

he single men rode away one evening and did not return,  violating Hackleman’s rule of no lone riders away from the train at any time. WF and Thomas  joined search parties the next day, but no sign of their travel companion was found by  sundown. Anxious to continue forward movement, Hackleman selected a panel of three older  men, including Thomas Morgan, to decide what to do with the man’s oxen, wagon and  possessions. The panel voted to assign the wagon and oxen to a large family of eight struggling  with an undersized wagon pulled by scrawny horses, and the man’s possessions were added to  Hackelman’s camp provision wagon for doling out to needy travelers during the later stages of  the trail. Five of the deaths occurred near the end of the journey. As was the norm for wagon  trains before 1850, the Hackleman train attempted to travel the fi

nce  where there was tension between the travelers and Natives during WF’s 1845 crossing.  Hackleman periodically sent out small hunting parties, to augment the food in the provision    286    wagon, led by one of his scouts and comprised of several male travelers handy with rifles. WF  reported that he never was invited on a hunt trip, but Thomas Morgan often participated.    In western Nebraska, a hunt party from the Hackleman train came upon a pack of pronghorn  deer in a ravine. Dismounted and creeping forward in the high grass, the group reached the lip  of the ravine, and stood to fire. To their astonishment, a half dozen well armed natives, likely  Sioux, rose from the grass even closer to the pronghorns, and turned to face the startled wagon  train men. The wagon train that transported Ira Goodman’s family was led by the  mayor of the town where the family lived, who was a banker by trade.
